lines.text: Undergrowth. That's what Book Two is called. And after everything Book One threw at us — the Fold, the Bris, Mairee, the Song — Nyland opens Book Two by walking us backwards. Forty cycles before the Unfolding. Sub-zero. Sterile. On the Yreus Relay Station.

Which we were told, for the entire first book, was uninhabited. That's already a reveal. The fact that Yreus was *manned* the whole time. The fleet charter said one-way street, safety measure — and Dennis Reed has been running experiments there for years.

And what an opening image. Behind the observation glass. Minus 54 degrees on the other side. Subject N. V. — Envee — sitting naked on a block of basalt. Bald. No eyebrows. Gray skin like volcanic ash. Returning his gaze with sad milky eyes.
The pronouns tell you everything. He calls her *Envee*. Envy.

He watches her scream against soundproof glass. She's forming his *name* with her lips. His thumb finds the PURGE toggle. But ends up pressing the other one. Was he about to purge her through the airlock? If so, why?
The wings? Two jagged slivers breaking through the gray skin between her shoulder blades. Wet, folded, shivering with the delicacy of a newborn. That's a phase change happening in real time.

And then Ian Perera walks out through the steam wall in a Köldur suit and carries her back in like a bride. *Ian Perera.* Joana's husband. From Book One. Turns out he's been in on this — forty cycles ago. What?! Why?

Which retroactively poisons every scene we ever had of that marriage. Every quiet moment in their kitchen. Everything Joana didn't know. And Reed's parting line, handing him the shim: 'No one must know. Not even your wife.'
The shim. That's the artifact. A carbon-fiber sliver etched with a symbol — 'a dark center with eight sharp arms radiating outward like spikes. Like antlers.'
Antlers. That's the Northern Mythical iconography. Reed is asking Perera to smuggle a shopping list for spinal fluids, pineal distillates, stem cells — to Kaspar Savannen. Milk and eggs.
Kaspar Savannen. Who by the time of Book One is already dead. Whatever Perera did with that shim forty cycles ago ended with the recipient in a frozen crypt.
Then Nyland jumps back to where part one ended. Post-Unfolding. Captain's quarters, FNS Dáinn. Ionie is reading Ben's log for the twelfth time.
Ben is asking her to *supply Yreus*. Breach its quarantine. Save them. Do it invisibly. But Ionie has nothing. Her ship is chained to anchor, waiting to be scrapped.
The impossibility of the request is the point. And Ben knows it. He signs off: 'I know what I'm asking.'
Then Ionie remembers Ben's advice. '*Make the impossible possible.*' And she remembers the thing he taught her — *inversion*. Think in the opposite direction.
She can't bring Mairee's resources to the station. So she'll haul the station to it.
It's a kōan move. The monk asks how to move a mountain. The master says: change your relationship to the mountain. Ionie doesn't solve the problem. She reframes it.
And then Bellamy calls, expecting to shut her down over the fuel manifests — and she leaves that call having *handed the Dáinn over*. 'Wiggle it how you will. I won't interfere.' What changed?
Ionie didn't beg. She listed what Yreus actually is — labs, life support, gold contacts, rare-earth composites, even fuel — and Bellamy's twitch stops.

Meaning she'd been holding something in. And Ionie has just given her permission to let it go. The line goes: 'And with whatever is going on below, I doubt Corbin will be in a position to stop you.' That last line is *loaded*.

Cut to Freya Homestead. Lysanne is hauling Vilde up out of stasis, dragging her past the crashed *Brisinger* — that funeral pyre of scorched alloy — past the locked Habs, past families pressing their palms silently against the glass. And the Grid pipelines respond.
'Phompf-phompf. Phompf-phompf.' The colony has become an organ. That sound is the machine drinking their distress.
And then Vilde walks into FOX. No resistance. Doors open. Operators half-up from their stations, kinetically indecisive.
And Vilde says four words that end the coup. 'Open the habs. All of them.' Not a speech. Not a vote. Just an order. Because the operators of FOX had been waiting for one.

Meanwhile — this is where it gets weird — Corbin is on a bench in a garden bed *far removed from the mob*. Counting purple alpine petals. Twelve. Thirteen. Fourteen. And something inside him starts to buzz.

The ego death sequence. And it's one of the most careful renderings of possession I've ever read. Nyland doesn't do it as violence. He does it as *tenancy*. 'He had existed as a passenger. Until now. The hemorrhage made space. The guest seeped through.'
The guest is Uræl. Æzal's older brother. And we watch him take the body like someone slipping on a coat that doesn't quite fit yet. He steps on the flowers. 'Sorry, little Colorsss.'

The sibilance is the tell. The throat is still Ulre's — the physical apparatus hasn't changed — but the *cadence* has. The mucus, the wet snort, the hand studying itself. 'The liver spots, the fine hair.
It's comedy. Dark, uncanny, magnificent comedy in the classical sense. And then the address to his brother across the smoke: 'Æzal. You dramatic little arsonist. What did you kindle this time?'
So when Ulre falls. Down the well. That's into his subconscious, losing control over his body, the chapter becomes something else entirely.

He meets an entity in the dark. And the entity says: 'You've been here before.' And then: 'When you learned that certain parts of yourself were not safe. You sent them here. One at a time. You were very thorough.'

Anyone who's read Jung's *Red Book* is smirking right now. This is *active imagination* — Jung's own method, dramatized as sci-fi possession. Around 1913 Jung descended into his own unconscious, met figures there, held conversations with them, and insisted they had autonomy. His guide-figure Philemon told Jung things Jung swore he had never put in his own head. That's what's happening to Ulre. And the entity? It's the shadow. Every part he exiled because it wasn't safe — the shame, the tenderness, the doubt — waiting for him in the basement. And now, its what Uræl used to develop its personality.
'Like you were wearing mine,' the entity says. Which hints again at his shadow. Ulre's suppressed personality, throwing it back at him.

Then Uræl scavenges the wreck of the *Brisinger*. And this section reads like a Tom Waits song. He finds a tarot deck. The Tower. The Hanged Man. Cards that read the same upside down. He rotates them. 'The tower held no allegiance to gravity.'

Seed envelopes — basil, cress, marigold, fennel. And one labeled *Magic*, thicker than the others, foil resealed with tape. Eight-sided dice made of bone and something 'shadowy and heavy.' Even the vibrator. He grants it a place in the bag. 'Fine.'

This is a being learning to inhabit a life and finding the life *amusing*. And then he sees the Humans building near the wreck — mycelia woven into the walls, bioluminescent wave following one of them — and Æzal reaches across for him. 'Uræl. Little brother. Is that you?'
The brothers are on the same planet again. And they are not on the same side. Uræl runs. Climbs the ridge. Finds an overhang. Says 'Home.' Eats a ration pack. And falls asleep.
So what can we expect from Undergrowth. What grows under a canopy. What grows under your skin.
What grows in the darkness if your own mind.
So that's what's been growing there the whole time...
